setup.zh: 七月，那一缕热卡在心口底下，沉不下去，账本末页的「下」字画不上圈。八月，马家花三百两给马小宝买了一张荐书，名册上还要马三画押。九月初四夜里，爹从墙上摘下了那张弓；娘给了你针线和一个空钱袋。
setup.en: In the seventh month the thread of warmth sticks under your heart and won't sink; the *down* on the ledger's last page can't get its circle. In the eighth, the Mas spend three hundred taels on a letter of recommendation for Ma Xiaobao, and the village roll still needs Ma San's signature. On the night of the fourth of the ninth month Father takes the bow down from the wall; Mother gives you needle and thread and an empty purse.

recap.zh: 爹把爷爷的弓给了你，娘给了你针线和一个空钱袋：「你自己挣满它。」
recap.en: Father gave you grandfather's bow, and Mother needle and thread and an empty purse: "Fill it yourself."

zh: 娘的针线，和一个空钱袋。
en: Father takes the old bow down from the wall.
Mother's needle and thread, and an empty purse.

story.zh:
七月里一个早上，小满去井上挑水，远远瞧见坡田那道石阶上有个人影，一级一级地往上跑，跑到顶，又跑下来。两根小辫子一甩一甩的，是阿禾。他走近了，听见她嘴里念念有词：「……四十一，四十二，四十三。」小满道：「大清早的，数台阶玩？」阿禾吓了一跳，一脚踩空，险些滚下来，站稳了，瞪他一眼：「数着玩。」「数了几遍了？」「……七遍。」她停了一停，又道：「三百级，得数七遍。」小满没听明白，还要问，她已经往坡下跑了，跑到坡底，回头喊了一句：「别告诉我娘！」他没告诉。可那天傍晚，阿禾她娘站在沈家门口，跟他娘借了一样东西：一把量鞋的尺子。

那天夜里，他娘头一回上了柴垛。她把那叠账纸摊在他膝盖上，一页一页往回翻：「满，手热」；「獐子一只，交马家半扇」；「满，夜里不打呼了」；一直翻到头一页，「满，十二。毛飞，落鸡窝。」「你往回看。」她道，「头一夜，你说人又不是鱼。」她又翻到最末一页，那十个字，三个圈：深，蓄，伸。「下」字外头，还空着。她拿指甲在那个「下」字底下轻轻划了一道，没划破纸：「它不来，是还没到日子。鸡抱窝，二十一天，你掀开看一回，就得多蹲三天。」小满看着那三个圈，没说话。他娘替他把棉絮往上掖了掖，手背碰着了他胸口那块木牌，停住了：「这牌子，怎么是温的？」小满道：「……我捂的。」他娘看了那块牌子好一会儿，道：「你捂的。」便下柴垛去了。

胡四把河湾里那场比憋气，当笑话讲给了马三。马三没笑，拿短棍敲着桌子想了一会儿，道：「憋气？县里开春贴了告示。沈家那小子，别是想去考仙门吧？」八月里，沉鼎观开山门的消息，传遍了四乡。马家老爷托了县里做书吏的远房表侄，花了整整三百两银子，给马小宝弄到了一张「荐书」。三百两，是沈家一百多年的租。马三在村口的酒桌上喝得满脸通红：「有荐书，灵根差一点也收！我家小宝，将来是要做仙师的！」马三一拍桌子，又道：「到时候，蒙山上的风——」村里人齐声接口，十分熟练：「姓马！」

荐书是马小宝一个人的，名册却是全村的。告示上写着「身家清白者」，县里派了一个老差役下乡收名册，一村一张，要村里的大户画押作保。石坳村的大户，只有马家。

差役是个瘦老头，骑一头瞎了一只眼的驴，一天要跑五个村，只想赶在天黑前吃上一口热饭。他在马家门口摊开名册，马三捏着笔，念一个名字，画一个押，念到「沈小满」，笔停了：「沈家欠着马家的租，不清白。这个押，不画。」差役看看马三，又看看日头：「欠多少？」马三张嘴就道：「前年的二十斤肉，今年的——」

「三爷。」小满他娘不知什么时候站在了人群前头，手里捧着那叠账纸，「前年欠的二十斤肉，去年秋天那头鹿，三爷家的家丁亲手称的；去年的租，是那张鹿皮；今年的租，秋收才到日子。去年冬月廿二，山风钱一百五十文，三爷亲手收的。」她一页一页地翻，一行一行地念，念得跟念经一样平。

差役接过账纸看了看，翻到末一页，指着那十个字：「这一页画了三个圈，是什么账？」四下里一静。小满站在人群后头，一颗心提到了嗓子眼。他娘面不改色：「鸡。抱窝的那只，蹲了一冬，孵出来三个，还有七个没出壳。」差役「哦」了一声，把账纸还给她，对马三道：「账是清的。画押。」他还要赶下一个村。

马三捏着笔，看了小满他娘很久，终于还是画了。画完了，他把笔往桌上一搁：「画了，也得爬得上去。三百级石阶，你家那小子，挑两桶水都喘。」

那天夜里，小满坐在柴垛上，咬着牙。「挑两桶水都喘」，这句话在他心口里打转，转一圈，那口气便往上一顶。他想起趴在后山的那个下午，他爹贴着他耳朵说：你心一跳，那口气就炸了。他便松了牙，不去压它，也不去数，只把那口气细细地吐，吐完了，再细细地吸，像他娘拨算盘，一颗是一颗。不知坐到了几更，心口底下那只卡了一夏天的水桶，忽然「咯噔」一声，自己往下走了：那一缕热沉过心口，沉到肚脐，一路暖到底，像一口热米汤咽下去，到了底，稳稳地落住了。再往下，便没了，像往一口枯井里扔了一块石头，等了半天，听不见响。他不知道那口井底下是什么，只知道这一回，热沉下去了，再没浮上来。

说书的在这里多一句嘴：世上的拳师、挑夫、水手、猎户，把喘气练到这一步，也就到了头——一身的灶烧得旺，风箱拉得匀，力气比旁人足些，活得比旁人长些，如此而已。修仙的人，偏偏从这里起步。那口井，凡人的身子上是没有门的。

第二天一早，他娘在账本最末一页的「下」字外头，画了第四个圈。画完了，把账本摊在炕桌上晾墨，自去灶前烧火。他爹拖着腿过来，低头看了半天。那十个字，他只认得这一个：山下、坡下、树底下，下套子的下。他拿粗指头在那个新圈旁边按了按，没敢碰着墨，问：「往下沉了？」小满道：「嗯。」他爹道：「那就趴得住了。」

过了两日，马小宝专程到沈家门口来了一趟。小满正蹲在院子里磨箭头。马小宝把那张盖着县衙大红印的荐书展开，冲他晃了晃：「看见没？有这个，灵根差一点也收。你有什么？」小满把磨好的那支箭举起来，对着日头照了照：「我有一支箭。」马小宝笑得桂花糕渣子喷了一地：「沈小满，你进得去，也是我的跟班；你进不去，就回来给我家放羊。反正，你这辈子，都在我后头。」

他走了。跟在他身后赶羊的，是刘豆芽。老刘五月里借的那两斗米，利滚利，到八月还不上，大小子便去马家放羊抵债。刘豆芽赶着羊从沈家门口过，没抬头，走出去老远，才回过头来，小声道：「沈小满，我原想跟你一块儿去泗水的。」

傍晚，阿禾在井台边上拦住他：「泗水几天的路？」「三天。」「一天吃几张饼？」「一张。」阿禾从耳朵上取下炭条，在那个蓝布面的小本子上记了一笔，转身走了。那本子，小满从没见过。

九月初四夜里，他爹坐在炕沿上，一只手按着膝盖，指头一下一下地敲着炕桌，敲了很久。然后他站起来，一瘸一拐地走到墙边，把那张缠着牛筋的旧弓摘了下来，放在儿子面前：「你爷爷的。你拿着。」小满道：「……爹，这话听着像骂人。」「不许瞎说。」他爹把弓往他怀里一塞，「你爷爷的弓。」

弓背上十七道牛筋，缠得紧紧的，是爷爷缠的，他爹重缠过的。这一年，两个同岁的孩子，一个在蒙山脚下，一个在千里之外的太一宫，各接过了一件前一个人留下的兵器：一个的鞘口里刻着一串划掉的名字，一个的弓背上缠着十七道牛筋。他爹道：「纪昌看了五年，才拉弓。你蹲了一年。」他顿了一顿，「往后一个人拉，没人在你身后说先看风了，你得自己说。还有一句，我没跟你说过：看不清风，就别拉。射出去的，收不回来。不拉，不丢人。」

小满听着耳熟，去年进山前一夜，他娘也说过一句差不多的：打不过就跑，跑不丢人。他爹又道：「到了仙家门派，要守人家的规矩。要老实。别跟人争——」他娘道：「他爹。」他爹便不说了。

他娘从怀里摸出一个小布包，是一套针线：一个顶针，三根针，一卷黑线，一卷白线。还有一个钱袋，青布缝的，针脚细细密密，袋口穿着一根红绳。钱袋是空的。「针线，衣裳破了自己补。」别人家的娘，临行密密缝；他娘把针给了他。她拿指头点了点那个钱袋，「钱袋是空的。你自己，挣满它。」

她看着他，又道：「你爹的话，你听一半。要守规矩——对。要老实——对好人老实。别跟人争——」说到这里，她停住了，伸手把他的衣领翻好，抻平了，才道：

「争得过，再争。」

油灯的火苗跳了一跳。她那只翻衣领的手，翻完了，在他的肩膀上停了一停。
story.en:
One morning in the seventh month Xiaoman went to the well for water and saw from far off a figure on the stone steps up to the slope field, running up step by step, reaching the top, running down again. Two little plaits flapping: A He. Closer, he heard her muttering: "…forty-one, forty-two, forty-three." Xiaoman said, "Counting steps for fun at the crack of dawn?" A He jumped, missed her footing and nearly rolled down; steadying herself, she glared at him. "For fun." "How many times?" "…Seven." She paused, then added, "Three hundred steps — you've got to count it seven times." Xiaoman didn't follow and was going to ask, but she was already running down the slope; at the bottom she turned and shouted: "Don't tell my mum!" He didn't. But that evening A He's mother stood at the Shens' door and borrowed something from his mother: a ruler for measuring shoes.

That night, for the first time, his mother climbed the woodpile. She spread the stack of account sheets on his knees and turned them back page by page: *Man: hands warm*; *One river deer, half to the Mas*; *Man: stopped snoring at night*; all the way back to the first page, *Man: twelve. Feather flew, landed in henhouse.* "Look back," she said. "That first night, you said people aren't fish." She turned to the last page: ten characters, three circles — *deep*, *store*, *stretch*. *Down* still bare. With her fingernail she drew a light line under *down*, not tearing the paper. "It isn't coming because it isn't time yet. A broody hen sits twenty-one days; lift her to look once and she sits three more." Xiaoman looked at the three circles and said nothing. His mother tucked the quilt up round him, and the back of her hand brushed the token on his chest and stopped. "Why is this token warm?" Xiaoman said, "…I warmed it." His mother looked at the token a good while. "You warmed it." And she climbed down.

Hu Si told Ma San the breath-holding as a joke. Ma San didn't laugh; he tapped the table with his club and thought a while. "Holding his breath? The county posted a notice this spring. That Shen boy — he isn't thinking of sitting the immortal gate, is he?" In the eighth month the news of Chending Temple opening its gate had spread through all the villages. Master Ma went through a distant nephew who was a county clerk and spent a full three hundred taels to get Ma Xiaobao a "letter of recommendation". Three hundred taels was over a hundred years of the Shens' rent. Ma San drank himself scarlet at the wine table at the village gate: "With a letter of recommendation, a bit of a bad root still gets you in! My Xiaobao's going to be an immortal master!" He banged the table again. "And then — the wind on Mount Meng —" The villagers took it up in chorus, well practised: "— is named Ma!"

The letter of recommendation was Ma Xiaobao's alone, but the roll was the whole village's. The notice said *of clean family*; the county sent an old runner round the villages to collect the rolls, one sheet a village, each to be signed as guarantee by the village's big household. Shi'ao Village's big household was the Mas, and only the Mas.

The runner was a skinny old man on a donkey blind in one eye, with five villages to do in a day and only one wish — a hot meal before dark. He spread the roll at the Mas' gate; Ma San held the brush, read out a name, signed; at *Shen Xiaoman* the brush stopped. "The Shens owe the Mas rent. Not clean. I won't sign this one." The runner looked at Ma San, then at the sun. "Owe how much?" Ma San opened his mouth at once: "The year before last's twenty catties of meat, this year's —"

"Third Master." At some point Xiaoman's mother had come to stand at the front of the crowd, holding that stack of account sheets. "The twenty catties of meat owed from the year before last — that deer last autumn, weighed by your own men. Last year's rent was that deer hide; this year's rent isn't due till the harvest. Last year, the twenty-second of the eleventh month, mountain-wind money, a hundred and fifty cash, taken by your own hand, Third Master." She turned page after page and read line after line, flat as reciting a sutra.

The runner took the sheets and looked through them, turned to the last page and pointed at the ten characters. "This page — three circles. What account is this?" Everything went quiet. Xiaoman, at the back of the crowd, had his heart in his throat. His mother didn't blink. "A hen. The broody one. Sat all winter, hatched three, seven still in the shell." The runner said "Ah," handed the sheets back, and told Ma San, "The accounts are clean. Sign." He still had another village to do.

Ma San held the brush and looked at Xiaoman's mother a long time, and in the end he signed. When he'd done he put the brush down on the table. "Signed — he still has to climb it. Three hundred stone steps, and that boy of yours pants carrying two buckets of water."

That night Xiaoman sat on the woodpile with his teeth gritted. *Pants carrying two buckets* — the words went round and round under his heart, and every time round, the breath shoved upward. He remembered lying on the back hill with his father's mouth at his ear: your heart jumps, and the breath bursts. So he unclenched his teeth, didn't press it, didn't count, only breathed out fine and thin, and in again fine and thin, like his mother at the abacus, one bead at a time. Some watch of the night he lost track of, the bucket that had been stuck all summer under his heart gave a *clunk* and went down by itself: the thread of warmth sank past his heart to his navel, warm all the way down, like a mouthful of hot gruel, and settled there, steady. Below that, nothing — like dropping a stone into a dry well and waiting, and hearing no splash. He didn't know what was at the bottom of that well; he only knew that this time the warmth had gone down and didn't float back up.

The storyteller will put in a word here: the boxers, porters, boatmen and hunters of this world who train their breathing this far have come to the end of it — the stove in them burns hot, the bellows pull even, they're a little stronger than others and live a little longer, and that's all. The immortals start from exactly here. That well has no door in an ordinary body.

Early next morning his mother drew a fourth circle on the last page of the ledger, round *down*, laid the book open on the kang table for the ink to dry, and went to light the stove. His father dragged his leg over and looked down a long while. Of the ten characters he knew only this one — down the hill, down the slope, down under the tree, setting a snare down. He pressed a thick finger beside the new circle without touching the ink. "Gone down?" Xiaoman said, "Mm." His father said, "Then you can lie still."

Two days later Ma Xiaobao made a special trip to the Shens' door. Xiaoman was squatting in the yard sharpening an arrowhead. Ma Xiaobao unfolded the letter with the county yamen's great red seal and waved it at him. "See this? With this, a bit of a bad root still gets in. What have you got?" Xiaoman held up the arrow he'd sharpened and sighted along it at the sun. "I've got an arrow." Ma Xiaobao laughed so hard he sprayed osmanthus-cake crumbs everywhere. "Shen Xiaoman, if you get in, you'll be my errand boy; if you don't, come back and herd my family's sheep. Either way, all your life, you'll be behind me."

He left. Driving the sheep behind him was Liu Douya. The two pecks of rice Old Liu borrowed in the fifth month had rolled up interest on interest and by the eighth month couldn't be paid, so his eldest went to herd the Mas' sheep to work off the debt. Liu Douya drove the sheep past the Shens' door without looking up; only when he was a long way off did he turn and say quietly: "Shen Xiaoman, I meant to go to the Si River with you."

At dusk A He stopped him at the well. "How many days' road to the Si River?" "Three." "How many flatbreads a day?" "One." A He took the charcoal from behind her ear, wrote a line in that little blue-covered notebook, and turned and went. Xiaoman had never seen that notebook before.

On the night of the fourth of the ninth month his father sat on the edge of the kang, one hand on his knee, tapping the kang table with a finger, a long time. Then he stood, limped to the wall, took down the old sinew-wrapped bow and set it before his son. "Your grandpa's. You take it." Xiaoman said, "…Dad, that sounds like swearing." "Don't talk nonsense." His father pushed the bow into his arms. "Your grandpa's bow."

Seventeen strips of sinew on its back, bound tight — bound by his grandfather, rebound by his father. That year two boys of the same age, one at the foot of Mount Meng and one in the Taiyi Palace a thousand li away, each took up a weapon left by the one before: one with a row of struck-out names cut inside its scabbard, one with seventeen strips of sinew wound round its back. His father said, "Ji Chang looked for five years before he drew the bow. You've crouched one year." A pause. "From now on you draw it alone; nobody behind you saying read the wind first. You'll have to say it yourself. And one more line I never told you: if you can't read the wind, don't draw. What's loosed can't be called back. Not drawing is no shame."

It sounded familiar to Xiaoman: the night before they went into the mountains last year, his mother had said much the same — if you can't win, run; running is no shame. His father went on: "At an immortal sect, keep their rules. Be honest. Don't fight with people —" His mother said, "Husband." His father said no more.

His mother took a little cloth bundle from her coat: a sewing kit — a thimble, three needles, a reel of black thread, a reel of white. And a purse, sewn of blue cloth, the stitches fine and close, a red cord through the mouth. The purse was empty. "Needle and thread — when your clothes tear, mend them yourself." Other boys' mothers stitch close and tight before the son sets out; his mother gave him the needle. She tapped the purse with a finger. "The purse is empty. You fill it yourself."

She looked at him and said: "Of your father's words, listen to half. Keep the rules — right. Be honest — honest with good people. Don't fight with people —" here she stopped, reached out and turned his collar straight, smoothed it flat, and only then said:

"If you can win, then fight."

The lamp flame jumped. The hand that had turned his collar, once done, rested on his shoulder a moment.

label.en: The sixth of the ninth month: set off for the Si River

exits.means: sets off for the trials at the temple

story.zh:
走的前一夜，小满去了一趟村东头。吴婆婆照旧坐在门槛上，拿一把破蒲扇一下一下地扇脚底下。他还没开口，她已道：「要走了。」小满在门槛边上坐下，等着她说那九句废话，好把那一句能救命的捞出来带走。吴婆婆却不说猫，也不说牙：「婆婆今儿不说废话了。只说一句。饿了，就吃。饱了，就放下。」小满等了一会儿：「……就这一句？」「就这一句。回罢。你娘在烙饼。」他觉得这一句比那九句废话还废，饿了吃，饱了放，三岁孩子都知道。走出去几步，吴婆婆在身后又道：「那块牌子，贴肉揣着。别叫它冷着。」他回头，她已经扇起了蒲扇，脸朝着西边，不再理他了。

那是他在柴垛上的最后一夜。他坐了一个时辰，数了一回：九十六。雁毛在他鼻子底下抖着，抖得很轻，像风过了以后，草尖上还剩下的那一点。没停。

九月初五。满，九十六。毛抖。

他娘把这一行写完，搁下了笔。一百二十，还差二十四。

临走前，他娘塞给他一个布包，里头是四张饼，是前一夜烙的。小满半夜醒来，看见灶间的油灯亮着——那灯芯头一回没掐短，火苗有指头那么大——他娘站在灶前，一张一张地烙。「路上吃。一天一张，吃到泗水。」小满数了数：「娘，到泗水三天，多了一张。」他娘道：「打不过，就跑。跑饿了，吃那一张。」她又塞给他一个小本子，是拿舅舅开春带来的那包红糖的包纸订的，一张一张裁得方方正正，封皮上还透着一点甜味。「一个人进山门，身上没个账本可不行。空的，你自己记。」一个空钱袋，一个空本子。小满把那根雁毛夹进了本子的第一页。

走的那天，是九月初六，天还没亮。舅舅在济世堂告了七天假，头天夜里便到了，要一路送他走到泗水；他爹送他们到县城。他娘没有送，她说家里得有人看着灶。她站在老槐树底下，两只手拢在袖子里，一动不动，像去年秋天那样。小满背着弓，揣着针线、空钱袋、空本子和四张饼，走过老槐树的时候，回头看了一眼。他娘的一只手从袖子里抬了起来，停在半空里，没有挥，也没有放下来。那一天碗碎的时候，他娘伸出去捞碗，也是这样停在半空里的。

他本以为阿禾会在那里，跟他算一算账，说一句「三个半，别忘了」。她不在。他又回头看了一眼，还是不在。羊坡上，刘豆芽赶着马家的羊，远远地朝他举了举鞭子。

他转过身，跟着他爹和舅舅往村外走去。离九月初九，还有三天；离一百二十，还差二十四。走出村口半里地，日头出来了，他忽然觉出胸口那块木牌是温的。白天，它向来是凉的；他两只手一直拢在袖子里，一回也没碰过它。他站住了，隔着衣裳按住它，心里头一回冒出一句话来：

……那是谁捂的？
story.en:
The night before he left, Xiaoman went to the east end of the village. Granny Wu sat on her threshold as always, fanning her feet with a tattered palm fan. Before he could speak she said, "You're leaving." Xiaoman sat down by the threshold, waiting for her nine sentences of nonsense, so he could fish out the one that could save a life and take it with him. But Granny Wu didn't talk about her cat, or her teeth. "Granny's not talking nonsense today. Just one sentence. When you're hungry, eat. When you're full, put it down." Xiaoman waited. "…Just that one?" "Just that one. Go home. Your mother's making flatbread." He thought that sentence more nonsense than the nine: eat when hungry, stop when full — any three-year-old knows it. A few steps off, Granny Wu spoke again behind him: "That token — keep it against your skin. Don't let it go cold." He looked back; she had taken up her fan again, facing west, and paid him no more mind.

It was his last night on the woodpile. He sat for an hour and counted once: ninety-six. The wild-goose down trembled under his nose, very lightly, like what's left on a blade of grass after the wind has passed. It didn't stop.

Ninth month, fifth. Man: ninety-six. Feather trembled.

His mother finished writing that line and put down the brush. A hundred and twenty, still twenty-four short.

Before he left, his mother pressed a cloth bundle on him with four flatbreads in it, made the night before. Xiaoman had woken in the middle of the night and seen the kitchen lamp lit — for the first time the wick not pinched short, the flame the size of a finger — and his mother at the stove making them one by one. "For the road. One a day, till you get to the Si River." Xiaoman counted. "Mum, it's three days to the Si River. There's one too many." His mother said, "If you can't win, run. When running makes you hungry, eat that one." She pressed on him a little notebook as well, made from the wrapping paper of the brown sugar his uncle brought in spring, the sheets cut square, the cover still faintly sweet. "Going through a temple gate alone, you can't be without an account book. It's empty; you write it." An empty purse, an empty notebook. Xiaoman pressed the wild-goose down between the pages of the first leaf.

The day he left was the sixth of the ninth month, before dawn. His uncle had taken seven days' leave from the Jishi Hall and arrived the night before, to walk him all the way to the Si River; his father would see them as far as the county town. His mother wasn't coming; someone had to mind the stove, she said. She stood under the old locust, both hands tucked in her sleeves, motionless, as she had the autumn before. Xiaoman, with the bow on his back and the sewing kit, the empty purse, the empty notebook and four flatbreads in his jacket, looked back as he passed the old locust. One of his mother's hands had come up out of her sleeve and stopped in mid-air — not waving, not lowered. The day the bowl broke, when his mother reached to catch it, her hand had stopped in mid-air just like this.

He'd thought A He would be there, to settle accounts with him and say "three and a half, don't forget". She wasn't. He looked back again; still not there. On the sheep slope Liu Douya, driving the Mas' sheep, raised his whip to him from far off.

He turned and followed his father and his uncle out of the village. Three days to the ninth of the ninth; twenty-four short of a hundred and twenty. Half a li past the village gate the sun came up, and he suddenly felt that the token on his chest was warm. By day it was always cool; both hands had been tucked in his sleeves all along, and he hadn't touched it once. He stopped, pressed it through his clothes, and for the first time a thought came to him:

…Then who warmed it?
